# Introduction

Many analyses need to know which features overlap which ranges. Reads are
assigned to genes. Peaks are matched to promoters. Variants are matched to
exons. In Bioconductor you do this with `findOverlaps()` and `countOverlaps()`
from `r Biocpkg("GenomicRanges")`.

GenomicRanges builds an index of the subject, called an NCList, each time you
call these functions. You can also build it once yourself with `GNCList()`.

`superintervalsr` gives you a different index for the subject, based on the
SuperIntervals algorithm. It stores intervals in one sorted array, with a
second small array that lets a query skip intervals that cannot overlap. This
is compact and fast to search. It helps most when you query the same
annotation many times, for example:

* annotating peaks from many samples against one set of genes
* counting overlaps for millions of reads
* scanning many windows across a genome

The package fits into existing Bioconductor code:

* `SuperIntervalMap()` takes a `GRanges` and returns an index. You pass it to
`findOverlaps()` or `countOverlaps()` in place of the `GRanges`.
* Chromosome and strand are matched as in GenomicRanges. The `Hits` you get
back point at rows of your original `GRanges`, so its metadata is easy to
recover.
* Options the index does not handle itself, such as `type = "within"` or a
`maxgap`, are passed on to GenomicRanges. You always get the same answer.

The package also has a lower-level `IntervalMap` class for plain integer
intervals. It adds operations such as merge, gaps and flank.

When should you use it? For a single query, plain GenomicRanges is simpler and
fast enough. When you query the same subject repeatedly, building a
`SuperIntervalMap` once makes each query faster. The README has timings
against both a plain `GRanges` and a prebuilt `GNCList`.

# Installation

Install from Bioconductor:

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("superintervalsr")
```

Building from source needs a C++17 compiler. The examples also use
`r Biocexptpkg("airway")` and `r Biocpkg("SummarizedExperiment")`. Install
these the same way.

```{r load, message = FALSE}
library(GenomicRanges)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
library(superintervalsr)
```

Some function names here, such as `count()`, `coverage()`, `gaps()` and
`flank()`, also exist in other packages. We load `superintervalsr` last so its
versions are used. Elsewhere, write `superintervalsr::count()` to be sure.

# Using SuperIntervalMap with GRanges

## A small example

Build the index once. The `GRanges` can span several chromosomes and both
strands.

```{r small-index}
genes <- GRanges(
    seqnames = c("chr1", "chr1", "chr1", "chr2"),
    ranges = IRanges(start = c(20, 1, 8, 1), end = c(30, 10, 18, 10)),
    strand = c("+", "-", "*", "+"),
    gene_id = c("GENE_C", "GENE_A", "GENE_B", "GENE_D")
)
gene_index <- SuperIntervalMap(genes)
gene_index
```

Use the index wherever you would use the `GRanges` subject:

```{r small-query}
peaks <- GRanges(c("chr1", "chr1", "chr2"),
    IRanges(c(5, 15, 40), c(8, 22, 45)), strand = "+")
hits <- findOverlaps(peaks, gene_index)
hits
countOverlaps(peaks, gene_index)
```

Subject hits are row numbers in `genes`. `as_granges()` returns the original
`GRanges`, so you can look up any metadata column:

```{r small-annotate}
overlapping_rows <- as(hits, "List")
mcols(peaks)$genes <- extractList(as_granges(gene_index)$gene_id,
    overlapping_rows)
peaks
```

The counts are the same as with `genes` as the subject:

```{r small-check}
stopifnot(identical(countOverlaps(peaks, gene_index),
                    countOverlaps(peaks, genes)))
```

Strand is used by default, and `"*"` matches either strand. To ignore strand:

```{r small-strand}
countOverlaps(peaks, gene_index, ignore.strand = TRUE)
```

## An RNA-seq example

The `r Biocexptpkg("airway")` data hold RNA-seq counts from human airway
smooth muscle cells, stored as a `RangedSummarizedExperiment`. Its
`rowRanges()` hold the exons of each gene.

The question: for the most highly expressed genes, which other genes overlap
their promoter?

First, turn each gene into one range covering all its exons, and add the mean
read count. Genes with exons on more than one chromosome or strand are
dropped.

```{r airway-data}
data("airway", package = "airway")

gene_spans <- range(rowRanges(airway))
single_span <- lengths(gene_spans) == 1L
gene_bodies <- unlist(gene_spans[single_span], use.names = FALSE)
names(gene_bodies) <- names(gene_spans)[single_span]
mcols(gene_bodies)$mean_count <- rowMeans(assay(airway))[single_span]
gene_bodies
```

We will query these gene bodies, so index them once:

```{r airway-index}
body_index <- SuperIntervalMap(gene_bodies)
body_index
```

Take promoters of the top 200 genes and find what they overlap:

```{r airway-query}
top_genes <- head(gene_bodies[order(-mcols(gene_bodies)$mean_count)], 200)
promoter_windows <- promoters(top_genes, upstream = 2000, downstream = 200)

promoter_hits <- findOverlaps(promoter_windows, body_index)
promoter_hits
```

Each hit links a promoter to a gene body. Every promoter overlaps its own gene,
so drop those and list the neighbours:

```{r airway-annotate}
neighbours <- data.frame(
    promoter_of = names(promoter_windows)[queryHits(promoter_hits)],
    overlaps_gene = names(gene_bodies)[subjectHits(promoter_hits)],
    neighbour_mean_count =
        mcols(gene_bodies)$mean_count[subjectHits(promoter_hits)]
)
neighbours <- neighbours[neighbours$promoter_of != neighbours$overlaps_gene, ]
head(neighbours)
```

Results can go straight back into the experiment. Here we store the number of
neighbouring genes in `rowData()`, so it stays with the counts:

```{r airway-rowdata}
top_se <- airway[names(top_genes), ]
other_genes <- countOverlaps(promoter_windows, body_index) - 1L
rowData(top_se)$promoter_neighbours <- other_genes
table(rowData(top_se)$promoter_neighbours)
```

Finally, check the hits match GenomicRanges, with and without strand:

```{r airway-check}
same_pairs <- function(a, b) {
    pairs_a <- sort(paste(queryHits(a), subjectHits(a)))
    pairs_b <- sort(paste(queryHits(b), subjectHits(b)))
    identical(pairs_a, pairs_b)
}
agree <- vapply(c(FALSE, TRUE), function(ignore) {
    same_pairs(
        findOverlaps(promoter_windows, body_index, ignore.strand = ignore),
        findOverlaps(promoter_windows, gene_bodies, ignore.strand = ignore))
}, logical(1))
stopifnot(all(agree))
```

## Things to know

* You get the same hits as GenomicRanges, sorted by query. Within one query
the order may differ.
* The index lives in C++ memory, so `saveRDS()` cannot save it. Save
`as_granges(index)` and rebuild after loading.
* The index does not change when you edit the `GRanges`. Build a new one.
* Circular sequences, such as the mitochondrial genome, are handled by
GenomicRanges. Ranges there can wrap past the end of the sequence.

# Plain intervals with IntervalMap

`IntervalMap` is the structure underneath `SuperIntervalMap`. It holds integer
intervals on one coordinate line, such as one chromosome. It ignores strand.
Each interval can carry any R value. Use it when you are not working with
`GRanges`, or when you need the extra operations below.

## Creating a map

Build a map from start and end vectors, a `data.frame`, or a `GRanges` on one
chromosome. Both ends of each interval are included, as in `IRanges`.

```{r im-create}
im <- IntervalMap(c(10, 15, 30), ends = c(20, 25, 40),
    values = c("Gene A", "Gene B", "Gene C"))
im

chr1_map <- IntervalMap(genes, seqname = "chr1", value_column = "gene_id")
chr1_map
```

You can also add intervals one at a time. Call `build()` when you are done
and before you query. The constructors above do this for you.

```{r im-add}
im2 <- IntervalMap()
add(im2, 10, 20, "Gene A")
add(im2, 15, 25, "Gene B")
build(im2)
```

`add()` and `build()` change the map in place. Unlike most R objects,
`im3 <- im2` does not make a copy.

## Querying a map

Each function returns a different view of the overlapping intervals:

```{r im-query}
has_overlaps(im, 12, 18)
count(im, 12, 18)
search_values(im, 12, 18)
search_items(im, 12, 18)
search_point(im, 35)
```

`search_idxs()` returns positions in the map. `at()` returns the interval at a
position. Positions follow the sorted order made by `build()`, not your input
order. To get back to your input rows, store the row number as the value.

```{r im-idx}
idx <- search_idxs(im, 12, 18)
at(im, idx[1])
```

## Many queries at once

Every call from R into C++ has a small cost. With thousands of queries, that
cost can outweigh the search itself. The `.batch` functions take vectors of
starts and ends and run every query in one call.

Both versions below give the same answer. The batch version skips the R loop:

```{r im-batch}
query_starts <- c(5, 12, 22, 35)
query_ends <- c(8, 18, 32, 50)

one_at_a_time <- vapply(seq_along(query_starts), function(i) {
    count(im, query_starts[i], query_ends[i])
}, integer(1))
all_at_once <- count.batch(im, query_starts, query_ends)

stopifnot(identical(one_at_a_time, all_at_once))
all_at_once
search_idxs.batch(im, query_starts, query_ends)
```

## Interval operations

These return a new map, ready to query. They work like `reduce()`, `gaps()`
and `flank()` in IRanges, but keep each interval's value.

```{r im-ops}
merged <- merge_overlaps(im)
search_keys(merged, 1, 50)

uncovered <- gaps(merged, 1, 50)
search_keys(uncovered, 1, 50)

windows <- expand(im, 5, 5, lo = 1, hi = 50)
search_keys(windows, 1, 50)

span(im)
```

Merging keeps one value per merged region. `intersection()` keeps values from
its first argument and can return overlapping pieces. Run `merge_overlaps()`
on the result to join them.

`coverage()` returns the number of overlapping intervals and their total
overlap with the query. Each interval counts on its own, so shared bases count
more than once.

```{r im-coverage}
coverage(im, 10, 40)
```

## Back to GRanges

`as_granges()` turns `search_items()` output into a `GRanges`. An
`IntervalMap` does not know its chromosome, so you supply it:

```{r im-granges}
chr1_items <- search_items(chr1_map, 5, 22)
as_granges(chr1_items, seqname = "chr1", valuename = "gene_id")
```
